title: Kids' Chemistry Sets: KABOOM!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of chemistry sets, from 18th-century "chemical chests" such as Johann Friedrich August Göttling's 1789 Garay chest and James Woodhouse's University of Pennsylvania sets, through 19th-century youth sets, the early 20th-century Kimcraft and Gilbert sets, and the 1950s-60s golden age tied to postwar American optimism about science. They cover dangerous experiments and contents (fire ink, zinc-sulfur flash, cyanide, iodine, the 1950s Atomic Energy Lab with uranium ore), gendered marketing to boys and the girls' Sachet Craft perfume set, safety regulation after the 1966 Child Protection Act, the decline and watering-down of sets from the 1980s, recalls such as Professor Wacko's Exothermic Exuberance (2001) and a 2007 fingerprint kit containing asbestos, and modern sets like the Kim C3000. The episode closes with a listener email from Halifax and the sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and childhood chemistry sets
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about who had chemistry sets as kids, mention Dave Reese's circuitry and a friend's TV show, and introduce the episode topic of chemistry sets.

segments.title: Eighteenth-century chemical chests
segments.summary: The hosts trace early chemistry chests, starting with Göttling's 1789 Garay chest with about 35 chemicals, a balance, mortar and pestle, a book of about 150 experiments, and platinum foil. They also describe James Woodhouse's University of Pennsylvania sets and the use of wineglasses before test tubes existed.

segments.title: Nineteenth-century youth chemistry sets and magic
segments.summary: Chemistry was linked to showmanship and magic. Frederick Accum's Chest of Chemical Amusement stressed safety, and by 1835 to 1856 sets such as the Eedies Youth Laboratory, Statham's Students Chemical Laboratory and Pike's Youth Chemical Cabinet were marketed to young people. Kingsley's Primus Chemical Magic and Practical Chemistry Cabinet came out in 1900, and the hosts explain the name Primus.

segments.title: Gen X kids and Primus band tangent
segments.summary: The hosts joke about kids who had chemistry sets and also learned magic or the Rubik's Cube, then have a playful exchange about the band Primus.

segments.title: Early twentieth-century sets and hazardous experiments
segments.summary: Chemistry sets were marketed to boys in the early 1900s. Kimcraft's 1916 set was a popular product, with a 1919 manual experiment that burned zinc and sulfur, fire ink made from potassium nitrate, and fuse-making. The hosts note hazardous chemicals such as iodine, ammonium nitrate, sodium cyanide and calcium hypochlorite, and a magic handkerchief trick with cobalt.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Ad break for the show's sponsors.

segments.title: Science clubs, Gilbert rivalry and early safety warnings
segments.summary: Sets came with science club memberships and magazines. Gilbert, rival to Kimcraft and maker of the Erector Set, sold a boys-only chemistry outfit. A 1936 Gilbert manual included safety warnings, and the hosts discuss parental involvement.

segments.title: Gender marketing and the girls' Sachet Craft set
segments.summary: Chemistry sets were marketed only to boys, with boys on packaging. Porter Chemical offered the Sachet Craft set for girls, a perfume-mixing kit. Gilbert later offered a girls' set in the 1960s, framed as training to become a lab technician.

segments.title: Golden age of chemistry sets in the 1950s and 1960s
segments.summary: The hosts describe the golden era, roughly the early-to-mid 1950s and 1960s, when postwar American optimism about science drove sales. Slogans from Kimcraft and Gilbert promoted science careers.

segments.title: Atomic Energy Lab and toy safety concerns
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the 1950 Atomic Energy Lab, which contained uranium ore, radiation sources, a Geiger counter, a spinthariscope and a cloud chamber. Only about five thousand were sold before it was discontinued. Nobel laureates credit chemistry sets, including Oliver Sacks's quote on risk. Accidents and environmental concerns led to a decline.

segments.title: Child Protection Act and the decline of chemistry sets
segments.summary: Congress passed the Child Protection Act in 1966. A 1968 HEW estimate put toy injuries at about 700,000 a year. Porter and Gilbert were bought by Gabriel Toys in 1967, and sets were watered down from the 1980s with plastic replacing glass and metal.

segments.title: Recalls: Professor Wacko's and asbestos fingerprint kit
segments.summary: A 2001 recall of Professor Wacko's Exothermic Exuberance involved unlabeled glycerine and potassium chemicals that caused house fires. A 2007 recall of a fingerprinting kit found up to five percent asbestos in its powder. A later 'Chemistry 60' set had no chemicals. Kary Mullis's experimenting is also mentioned.

segments.title: Modern chemistry sets for adults and homeschoolers
segments.summary: Dave found modern sets, including the Kim C3000 at about $2,880 plus chemicals, which the Wall Street Journal rated best overall in 2006. Some sets cover a full year of eleventh-grade chemistry, and meth labs were cited as a reason for watering down sets.

segments.title: Listener email from Matt in Halifax
segments.summary: Matt, a listener from Halifax, Nova Scotia, says he has listened to the whole back catalog and is training for ultramarathons. He announces a new baby and asks for a live show in Halifax. The hosts respond and give the email address.
